growth_story.headline: Nigeria's oil-fuelled boom of the 2000s ended in 2015; income per person then fell until 2021 and has recovered slowly since, helped by reforms from 2023.
growth_story.arc: Nigeria's income per person slipped in the 1990s, by -0.3 percent a year over 1990–1999, and the sources used here say little about why. From 2000 to 2014 it grew 4.2 percent a year, as oil prices rose, steadier economic management and reforms in banking and telecoms gave private firms confidence, and services grew fast. That run ended in 2015: oil prices fell, security worsened and earlier reforms were reversed, and income per person shrank by 4.0 percent in 2016 and by 8.3 percent in 2020, when oil slumped again and COVID-19 hit. Across 2015–2025 growth averaged -0.7 percent a year, leaving income per person 8.4 percent below its 2015 peak and about where it first was in 2011. Since 2023, reforms that ended fuel subsidies, freed the exchange rate and stopped central bank financing of the deficit have steadied the economy, and income per person has grown every year since 2022, by 1.9 percent in 2025.

threads.title: Oil boom and early reforms
threads.text: In the 2000s high oil prices came together with steadier economic management and reforms in banking and telecoms. Private firms, especially in services, grew fast enough to shrink oil's share of the economy, and income per person grew 4.2 percent a year over 2000–2014.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and World Bank describe strong reforms and a steadier economy since 2023, yet in the data income per person grew only 1.9 percent in 2025 and is still about where it first was in 2011. The gap is population growth: the World Bank found GDP growth in 2015–2021 much lower than the pace at which the population grew, so headline growth overstates gains per person.
